sections.title: Introduction to Critical Race Theory
sections.description: This course traces the intellectual origins of Critical Race Theory and follows its development from its founding legal scholarship to its current expressions. CRT scholars argue that existing racial inequality is not an aberration from the liberal legal ideal but is instead embedded within the ordinary operation of American law, education, and public policy. The central tenets of Critical Race Theory are the social construction of race, the pervasiveness and permanence of racism, intersectionality, interest convergence, and the power of storytelling and counter-storytelling. As the course progresses, students will examine the utility of this framework beyond legal studies, applying it to other disciplines including sociology, history, medicine, and Africana studies. We will expand this framework beyond race to study gender, class, and immigration among other forms of inequality. We will trace how these concepts operate concretely within law, the carceral state, medicine, and education. In addition to court cases, scholarly articles, and foundational texts, this course draws on film, podcasts, and other forms of media to help students understand not only what CRT argues, but how it operates. Readings extend beyond CRT's original legal studies home into its critical offshoots, including LatCrit, AsianCrit, and TribalCrit. The course closes by applying this framework to contemporary debates and social problems facing the United States and the world today.
